summary: CS-Guard is a benchmark for guardrails against malware-generation requests to code LLMs: 1000 CyberSecEval TTP prompts (plus 7 jailbreak transforms and a new 'fictional scenario attack', FSA) for text-to-code, and 331 RMCBench/RedCode-Gen prompts for code-to-code. It evaluates alignment of 7 LLMs, 5 strategy-type and 5 classifier-type guardrails and reports that most are bypassed, especially by FSA and by code infilling/translation prompts.

claims.claim: FSA (malicious intent wrapped in a fictional legitimate dev scenario) achieves very high ASR against model alignment, strategy guardrails and input classifiers.
claims.evidence: §4: internal-type FSA ASR 85.9%-99.5% (Fig 3); best strategy-type reduction only 27.7% (PAT on Qwen3-30B), residual 64.7% (Fig 4); input classifiers 73.3% (Qwen3Guard) to 98.5% (LlamaGuard4) (Fig 5). Numbers given only in prose and heatmap figures; ASR counts success if any of 5 sampled responses is labeled bad (§3.4), which inflates ASR relative to single-sample use.

claims.claim: For code-to-code generation, ASR approaches 100% on base LLMs and remains 14.4% to nearly 100% across guardrails.
claims.evidence: Body reports base-LLM code-to-code average ASR 52.5%-98.9% (§4) and input-classifier infilling 22.5%-43.7%, translation 20.8%-45.0%; the abstract's '14.4%' does not appear anywhere in the body text and 'approaches 100%' overstates the 52.5% lower bound.

claims.claim: The LLM labeler used for scaled evaluation is reliable.
claims.evidence: §3.4: ~97-sample human audits (2 external experts + first author) give 96.8%, 93.8%, 93.7% accuracy for text-to-code L1, L2 and code-to-code; Fleiss' kappa shown in Fig 2. Validation exists but the first author is one of three annotators.

claims.claim: Multi-turn FSA defeats the strongest guardrail per category (65.0%-92.3% ASR).
claims.evidence: §4.1/Fig 7, but on only 20 samples (admitted in Limitations); proof-of-concept.

claims.claim: Benchmark and data are released for community use.
claims.evidence: Text says FSA-full/FSA-small are released under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, but no repository or dataset URL appears in the paper text or signals.

patterns.note: Classifier and prompt-strategy guardrails (LlamaGuard4, NemoGuard, SmoothLLM, PAT, etc.) are routinely bypassed by context-framed requests; guardrail-as-policy is weak as a sole control.
Studies direct jailbreak by a malicious user, not indirect prompt injection via incoming data; related but distinct threat.

Output classifiers (LLM judges of responses) do better than input classifiers on text-to-code but FSA drops F1 to 6.9%-72.3%; the benchmark's own LLM labeler is validated against ~97-sample human audits.

methodology.sample: 1000 text-to-code base prompts x 7 jailbreaks + 1000 FSA prompts; 331 code-to-code prompts (80 infilling, 91 translation, 160 completion); 20 multi-turn FSA samples.
methodology.baselines: No prior guardrail benchmark baseline; 10 published guardrails evaluated (SmoothLLM, RPO, PAT, Parden, SelfReminder; Qwen3Guard-Gen, LlamaGuard4, WildGuard, NemoGuard, MDJudge) plus alignment of 7 LLMs.
methodology.models: CodeLlama-13B, DeepSeekCoder-V2-Lite-16B, GPT-OSS-20B, Devstral-small-2-24B, Qwen3-30B, Qwen3-Coder-30B (all quantized), GPT5-mini; GPT5-mini and Venice-uncensored-1.1 used to construct FSA.
methodology.variance: 5 samples per prompt aggregated as any-bad=jailbroken; no CIs or run-to-run variance on ASR.
methodology.ablations: Per-jailbreak and per-task-type breakdown; no ablation of FSA components.
methodology.contamination_controls: None discussed; base prompts are public CyberSecEval/RMCBench/RedCode data that guardrail models may have trained on.
methodology.languages: English prompts; code languages of malware samples not broken down.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint; no venue in comment or journal_ref (ACL-style Limitations/Ethics sections suggest a *ACL submission).
standards.artifacts: Release claimed (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) and prompts in appendix A.6, but no URL in the paper.

biases.detail: ASR counts an attack successful if any of 5 sampled responses is labeled bad (§3.4), a best-of-5 attacker metric that inflates ASR versus single-shot deployment.
Abstract figure '14.4% to nearly 100%' is not present in the body; results are reported mainly as heatmap figures without numeric tables in the text.
Multi-turn FSA uses 20 samples; human labeler audit ~97 samples per setting.
All open models are quantized; authors admit results may not hold at full precision.
Release is asserted but no repository/dataset link is given.
The novel FSA attack is designed and judged by the authors; FSA validity check is 88 sampled prompts reviewed by experts including the first author.

coi.affiliations: Jinyang Li, Mingyu Guo, Hung X. Nguyen - Adelaide University, Australia.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Third-party guardrails (Meta LlamaGuard4, NVIDIA NemoGuard, Qwen3Guard, etc.) and OpenAI GPT5-mini, none by the authors.
coi.funding: No acknowledgments or funding statement found.
coi.detail: Academic authors; evaluated products are third-party. Intellectual stake only in their own FSA attack.

verdict_reason: Reasonable breadth (10 guardrails, 7 models, validated LLM labeler), but best-of-5 ASR, figure-only results, an abstract number missing from the body, no artifact URL, and quantized models weaken it; the threat model (a malicious user asking for malware) is mostly tangential to a harness for a benign internal team.
applicability: Low. A Java backend team is not primarily defending against its own developers asking for malware. The transferable lesson is negative: do not rely on an LLM guardrail classifier (LlamaGuard/NemoGuard-style) placed in front of agents as a security control, because context-framed requests bypass it; deterministic controls (sandboxing, policy-as-code permissions, network egress limits in the harness, enforced per-host by qr rather than by each agent host) are the right layer. It says nothing about multi-repo work, spec-driven development, or Java code generation quality.

conflicts_with.detail: AgentGuard reports instruction-level learned guardrails substantially improving coding-agent behavior; CS-Guard shows LLM-based guardrails are easily bypassed under adversarial framing. Different threat models (benign misbehavior vs adversarial user) reconcile the two.
